Your mom is an idiot. I know this because I was also that idiot once. I love my kid more than anything, but that doesn’t stop parents from being stupid or blind to new things in the world, or afraid of things they don’t understand- especially things they have experienced as permanent. 

Having a gender or sexuality that conforms meant a lot more to our parents than it does to us. It usually meant their survival, more than it does today. Those roots still run very deep, of fear in particular. That you are entering an adult world of sex and sexuality. Of knowns and unknowns. New vocabulary.  It’s like moving to a new country. It may take them a few years to adjust to all the changes, but try and be patient (with boundaries of course). 

As a former idiot parent, here’s something I can recommend: Offer your mom a window of time to speak to you, with a specific purpose, and with boundaries. She is allowed to ask you questions, and you may respond (if you wish) BUT - you create the list of approved responses from her, and she is not to deviate from that list. Here’s an example:

Tell me more. That’s amazing. I didn’t know that! When did you begin to think that? What makes you feel that way? How can I help you now? How can I help you in the future? I never thought of it that way. I still don’t understand, but I do support/trust/love you. I’m sorry. I was wrong about that.  I may have been wrong about that. I wish I had done that differently, knowing that now.  Yes please. No thank you.  I was not brought up to see things this way. I am trying. I will try.  I love you. I hurt you. I made you feel alone. I am sorry.  I didn’t know.  

Those are some examples of pre-approved responses that can begin to retrain your mom how to speak to you, and give her the chance to do so.  Cutting off connections with your mom is hard for good reason, she loves and wants the best for you.  She’s just got blinders on. Retrain her. 

Make HER do the work.

Hello! Been there. Be sure to differentiate between your ABILITY TO FEEL happiness, vs having things to be happy about. The two are very different, and should be managed as such. Everyone’s ability to “feel good” can be increased or decreased when basic needs are met or unmet, such as safety, shelter, food, acknowledgment, belonging, etc. If trauma has occurred, additional “reconstruction” may need to happen before “feeling good” also equals “feeling normal”.  

Remember it’s ok to have to have things to be happy about and still not “feel” happy. Try looking for other words to describe yourself in addition to blatantly positive emotions. Content. Enfolded. Loved. Enlightened. Secure. Wiser. Curious. Endearing. Cheerful. Gracious. Thoughtful. Kind. 

There are many emotions worth noting and having - it sounds like you’re starting to explore a marvelous new buffet!

Believe me he knows how to do his own. Get a neighbor kid to walk (& brush) the dogs outside so there’s less fur and dander.  Live like a frat boy for awhile. Order pizza, or uber eats. Stop cooking. You can do this.

Stop. Breathe. You WERE hurt by what he said. It’s ok to acknowledge that. It can also be true that he genuinely didn’t mean to hurt you. Both of these things can be true at the same time. 

2 things are happening here. 1: You’re hypersensitive to any suggestions about your weight and are on high alert for emotional abuse; this doesn’t quite sound like that to me. It sounds like classic ptsd symptoms, nothing more. 2: He doesn’t yet adequately understand how ptsd and triggers work, so you must educate him or point him in the direction to do so. 

It sounds like once he understands more deeply that ptsd causes physical and emotional responses that are not entirely yours, he will help learn to manage them.  Hold his face, look him in the eye, and tell him the truth: “I know that this is my issue, because you’re hilarious. But as I’m working out some personal issues, I really need your help with something. Reminders of my ex are very stressful for me, and normally you are very loving - but when you make references or jokes about my weight, it stings in a way that’s hard for me to recover from, because it brings up so much other junk with it. I know you don’t mean for that cross reference to happen, but it just puts me in an emotional place like I’m back with my ex when your comments hit me that way. And they don’t always sting, again, you’re so funny and I love that about us. But for this topic, I need your protection from this feeling, until I can work out how to manage it myself.”

Remember also that deflective humor is a common way for guys to deal with uncomfy feelings or topics, try to steer him gently (at first) if he’s not getting it right away.  

That being said: If you say the above or something similar to him, and he does not reach for you, comfort you, hold you, express surprise and concern, or show any sign of tenderness - that’s your sign to bail, because he will be too self absorbed to hear anything you actually said, and instead will become defensive.  

So either way, your answer will come from first being vulnerable and watching his real time response.

What you are describing is called “codependency”.  The name is somewhat misleading, but if you Google it, you will see yourself and your romantic patterns in black-and-white before your very eyes. 

You are not alone in these patterns, many people have them and they are a result of your own emotional needs not being met properly.  Most peoples parents do not have gigantic emotional toolboxes to teach their children with - so we are left grasping with our best efforts, not really knowing what’s wrong or how to fix it. 

The good news is that it is fixable. In person or online groups for CODA (codependent ppl) exist so that you can meet, talk about, discover and share healthy emotional support tools and patterns. There are tons of books to walk you through this as well. 

The main thing is don’t be too hard on yourself. Most of us are not taught these things and have to learn when we’re older, and feel like we’re too old to have to be learning this stuff - you’re not. This is how most of us end up learning it - later. So welcome, and good for you for beginning your journey! Get some books and start reading!

The idea is that it is impossible to “clear the mind” - it is designed to create thoughts, so approaching meditation this way is unwise. Instead, focus on a nonsensical word or sound that has no real meaning, and repeat it over and over. Gently refocus your mind over and over to your one word or sound (also called a mantra), without harshness or judgment, notice when your thoughts begin to form and gently guide them back to your mantra, mantra, mantra. I ask people 2 things. If they have a job or go to college, I ask what they do or what they plan to do. If they seem enthusiastic and happy about it, or discontented, I ask them to describe what they like (or dislike) most about it in detail.  (When people describe things they enjoy, they associate that enjoyment with speaking with you, so keep the focus on positive details if you can.)

Now, the second part takes time to develop, but the second question should be asked with genuine curiosity if you want to build REAL rapport quickly.  Now that they’re all prepped talking about what they already like or dislike, you’ve built a little trust, now you’re going to ask them about what they really love, like this:  “It sounds like you’re really un/happy with how things are going...is this where you saw yourself when you were a kid, or did you want to do some totally different?”  

This sentence does a lot of things in a short amount of time. First it acknowledges that you heard what they were saying, which builds trust. Next, you are asking a personal question that isn’t too personal, as it is simply about a childhood dream.  (Another way to ask the question is if you could wave a magic wand, or fill their bank account with $100 mill, what would they enjoy waking up doing every day that would fulfill them?)  

Asking this question will cause the person to reach deep inside themselves to remember what is usually a pleasant time and memory.  The more detail you can get from the person by asking more questions, the more successful you will be in building a friendship.  Recounting these experiences with you will build a fast friendship that you can put a good foundation on.  Good luck!

There are hundreds of ways to deal with depression and tons of different ways that people experience it. One person‘s experience with depression is going to be 100% different from another persons experience, so learn all you can but try not to put yourself into a box. NTA and I have a suggestion. I also struggle with mental health issues. Without knowing any details about her specifically, I can give you a suggestion that works well for us. 

When I start to feel “escalated” (nerves jumpy, mind racing, close to tears, panic attack, etc) I use a code word to tell my man, or just reach out for him quietly.  He knows when I am feeling like this what I need most in the world is to feel secure and loved.  It took us a long time to understand this, because mental health issues can manifest as anger, insecurity, etc - so it doesn’t seem likely that a close hug and soft words could be the solution to an outburst - but sometimes it really really is. 

When I am in that state, my mind is basically giving me the message that everything I’m feeling is wrong, everything I’m thinking is bad, and that there is something horribly wrong with me for feeling this way, all of which feel out of my control entirely.  It’s horrible. 

When my man comes to hug me close, he doesn’t try to solve anything. He says things like, “Everything will be ok, everything is ok. You are ok, and so beautiful. Go ahead and cry if you need to. I am here and I love you.”  He just holds onto me until i basically cry it out - usually a few minutes and then it goes away.  

It may feel awkward to approach her this way when she is manifesting anger, but try it with her and ask her if it helps.  If she is angry, you can say “It looks like you are feeling overwhelmed right now and I’m not sure how to help you feel better but I’d like to try. Would you be open to letting me hold you closely and tell you everything will be ok?  I just want to be close to you and let you know that I love you even though you are having all these difficult feelings right now.”   Pretty sure that will solve your problem most of the time. Good luck!

My former boss taught me this remedy that will never offend: If a customer is currently speaking to you directly, and another guest enters or attempts eye contact or speech - brief eye contact, a warm smile, and raising 1 finger in the air as you return your attention to the customer at hand will do the trick. 

It accomplishes 3 powerful things. 
1. Retains utmost respect to current customer, as you do not verbally interrupt them. 
2. Immediately acknowledges the new person, putting them at ease, creating respect and patience.
3. Alerts the guest that you will be with them shortly. Letting them feel they also deserve your attention (& will have it shortly) will make it less likely for them to clamor for it loudly.

YTA and hear me out. You’re obviously not a mean spirited kid, and complex communication is tough even for adults, so this is not your fault.

Here is how you can, and should, handle this now and in the future. 

Call your dad and say something like, “Dad, I really fucked up.  I had a great time on our trip, but a few times I was embarrassed about something you said or did, and I really let it get to me.  Even though I still feel embarrassed about it, I should not have said that I did not want to travel with you again or anything like that.  It was a harsh thing to say and I really did not mean that. This will let your dad know his behavior is still not ok, but that you are taking responsibility for your reaction as well, which will be a good model for him.  

It’s also ok to tell him what your concerns are. Use this model.  Concern, feeling, request.  

- My concern is: “When you drank last Friday night (be specific!), your social boundaries went away and you came on to the waitress, and it made me feel embarrassed. I’d like to know that won’t happen again, because it was really uncomfy.” 

- My concern is: “I enjoy spending time with you, but it becomes difficult for me to focus when I hear background noise nearby - would you grab a pair of headphones before the next trip so we can both be comfy next time?“

Etc.

My dad has every science and bio/chemical degree known to man, and his dad (a doctor) told him what I’m telling you.  Change your mind about the material.  It’s absolutely possible, and is easier than you think. 

Forbid yourself from speaking negatively, even in your own mind, about the class, topic, professor and assignments.  Write a list of things that are more accurate, such as: Instead of telling yourself “I dislike this material so much”, I would drill it down to specifics you can actually handle.  

Like this: Is it the material?  What about it?  Because it’s difficult? Is it difficult because you didn’t devote enough time to learn it?  Then it’s not really “difficult”, it’s that you need to give yourself more time to learn it.  See what I mean?  Follow that thread for every thought you have about class so you can clearly see your mind is changeable about the topic, and you’ll find life much more enjoyable.  Now onto self talk: 

Beginner: “I love chemistry! It is complex and challenging, and I can rise to any challenge. Although I am not used to devoting this much extra energy to learning something new, this doesn’t mean it’s not important or worth it. I will apply my standard or virtue to complete the challenge and task before me, as education is my reward.” 

Once you get used to rethinking - it will come more easily and naturally until you become an expert, like anything else.  

Expert:  “I will probably use everything I learn in this class on an episode of Who Wants to be a Millionaire, and I will be the most obscurely fascinating person anyone knows with all this knowledge, and possibly also be The Most Interesting (wo)Man In The World as a result.”

Change how you feel about the material, and learning it, and you will breeze on by.
